So, how do we reconcile the statement that the long-arm statute ‘‘go to the limits of due pro- cess’’ with the fact that the statute contains specific provisions that limit the court’s jurisdiction? The answer is that the court will construe the long-arm statute as broadly as possible, but not beyond its terms. If the language of the statute can be construed to support jurisdiction, the court will do so. But it won’t stretch the language of the statute to support jurisdiction, even if it would be constitutional to do so. So, in this case, the court will likely conclude that Ausable isn’t subject to jurisdiction under the long-arm statute, because it hasn’t ‘‘transacted business’’ in the state. It will dismiss the case for lack of jurisdiction, even though it would be constitutional to exercise jurisdiction. This is the meaning of the phrase ‘‘the long-arm statute goes to the limits due process.’’ It means that the court will construe each provision of the long-arm statute as broadly as it can, without exceeding the constitutional limits on jurisdiction. It doesn’t mean that the court will exercise jurisdiction whenever it would be constitutional to do so, regardless of whether the long-arm statute supports it. So, C is wrong. The case will be dismissed, but not because it would be unconstitutional. It will be dismissed because the long-arm statute doesn’t authorize it. A is also wrong. The court will not likely conclude that Ausable is subject jurisdiction under the ‘‘transacting business in New York’’ provision of the long-arm statute. It hasn’t transacted business there.
